periods.section_anchor: How Do We Learn About the Past?
materials: Chapter summary handout or textbook (Fig. 4.1 reference)
periods.visual_aids: Visual timeline of life on Earth (Fig. 4.1) showing formation of planet, first cells, bacteria, plants, fish, reptiles, mammals, humans

time_bands.activity: Students write down their earliest personal memory in one or two sentences and then share with a neighbour. The teacher asks: if memories are personal history, what tools do we use when no one alive remembers? This positions the chapter's central question without yet naming the scholars.

The teacher displays Fig. 4.1 and walks through its major markers — planet formation, first cells, bacteria, plants, fish, reptiles, mammals, Homo sapiens — pausing to ask: 'Where on this line do humans appear? What does that tell us about the depth of Earth's history?' Students mark the fraction that humans occupy on a quick sketch of the timeline in their notebooks.

Students receive a four-row table (columns: Scholar, What they study, Example of evidence they use) and must fill in geologists, palaeontologists, anthropologists and archaeologists from the text. For each scholar, they write one concrete example: soil or river features for geologists, fossil footprints or plant impressions for palaeontologists, living and ancient cultures for anthropologists, excavated tools or pots for archaeologists.

Pairs compare their tables and resolve any differences by returning to the text. The teacher cold-calls two groups to read one row each, then asks: 'Why might historians need all four types of scholars rather than just one?' Students offer reasons aloud.

periods.section_context: Life on Earth timeline, geologists, palaeontologists, anthropologists, archaeologists, fossils
periods.teacher_notes: The chapter begins by anchoring historical inquiry in the enormously long story of life on Earth before humans appear, so the visual timeline is central to establishing scale. A common confusion is that archaeologists and palaeontologists do the same work — stress that palaeontologists study fossils from millions of years ago while archaeologists excavate objects people left behind, a meaningful difference. Encourage students to notice that no single scholar type can reconstruct the full picture.

periods.activity_title: Calendars and the CE / BCE System
periods.section_anchor: How Is Time Measured in History?
periods.visual_aids: Fig. 4.3 timeline spanning 300,000 BCE to present with marked events

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'If you wanted to record when your grandfather was born, you would write a year — but which calendar's year?' Students call out systems they know (Gregorian, Islamic, Hindu pañchānga, Chinese). The teacher lists these on the board and notes that different societies anchored their calendars to different significant events, such as a ruler's birth or start of a reign.

The teacher introduces CE and BCE: CE counts forward from the conventional birth date of Jesus Christ, replacing AD; BCE counts backward from the same date, replacing BC. Students write two anchor examples — 1947 CE for India's independence, 560 BCE for the approximate birth of Gautama Buddha — and draw a simple number line with the BCE side extending left and the CE side extending right, marking both events.

The teacher poses the Let's Explore calculation problem: 'There is no year zero in the Gregorian calendar — 1 BCE is immediately followed by 1 CE. So how many years passed between 560 BCE and 2025 CE?' Students work individually, then the teacher guides the class to the formula: add the two numbers and subtract 1 (560 + 2025 − 1 = 2584 years). Students try a second example: from 100 BCE to 100 CE.

The teacher explains century and millennium: any 100-year block counted from 1 CE forward or 1 BCE backward is a century; a millennium covers 1,000 years. Students identify which century 1947 CE falls in (20th) and which the current year falls in (21st), then locate three events on Fig. 4.3 and write each event's century. The unit closes by noting that Indian pañchāngas combine solar and lunar positions to give festival dates and eclipse predictions, illustrating that multiple calendar systems serve real purposes alongside the Gregorian system.

periods.section_context: CE, BCE, Gregorian calendar, century, millennium, pañchānga, Fig. 4.3 events
periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse BCE and BC, or assume BCE counts forward like CE — the number line sketch and the no-year-zero formula address both errors directly. The pañchānga reference is not peripheral detail but illustrates that calendar plurality reflects genuine scientific and cultural traditions. The BCE-to-CE calculation exercise is the constitutive skill of this section and deserves unhurried attention.

competency_edges.competency_text: Representing and analysing historical data in timeline form, including CE/BCE date calculation
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct a number-line timeline, position dated events correctly in CE and BCE, and calculate elapsed time across the CE/BCE boundary.

periods.section_anchor: How Is Time Measured in History?
materials: Blank A4 paper or notebook pages
periods.visual_aids: Fig. 4.3 timeline as a model of timeline layout

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly revisits the CE/BCE number line and the century-counting rule introduced in the previous unit on calendars. Students are asked: 'What sources might a historian use to reconstruct your family's history since 1900 CE?' — photographs, diaries, ID cards, relatives' memories. This question bridges chronological method to personal evidence.

Each student draws a horizontal timeline from 1900 CE to the current year, marking it in 25-year intervals. They place at least five family events (births, migrations, marriages, significant changes) at their correct positions, labelling each event and identifying the source they would consult to verify it (photograph, relative's account, certificate). The teacher circulates, prompting: 'Is that event in the 20th or 21st century? Which decade?'

Students pair up and explain one event on each other's timeline, stating: what the event is, when it occurred, and which source confirms it. Partners ask at least one question that challenges the placement — for example, 'How confident are you in that date, and why?'

The class discusses: 'When sources are missing or memories conflict, how do historians decide what happened?' The teacher draws the connection to how professional historians face the same problem with ancient timelines, setting up the next section's work on historical sources.

periods.section_context: Family timeline construction, sources for personal history, century and decade placement
periods.teacher_notes: The Let's Explore family-timeline activity in this section asks students to apply the CE/BCE and century-counting skills from the prior work on calendars to their own lived context. A common difficulty is students placing events without identifying any verifying source — press them to name a specific source for each event rather than guessing. The closing discussion about conflicting sources anticipates the taxonomy of historical sources treated in the next section without naming it.

competency_edges.competency_text: Representing and analysing historical data in timeline form, including CE/BCE date calculation
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can place events on a scaled timeline, assign century labels, and assess the reliability of the source behind each placement.

periods.activity_title: Mapping the Taxonomy of Historical Sources
periods.section_anchor: What Are the Sources of History?
materials: Textbook page showing the sources taxonomy diagram
periods.visual_aids: Sources taxonomy diagram: Archaeological, Inscriptions, Oral, Indian Literature, Foreign Accounts, Artistic Sources

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with the Let's Explore family-tree prompt: 'When you reconstructed your family's past, you used photographs, diaries and relatives' memories — what category of source is each?' Students suggest groupings. The teacher then defines a source of history as any place, person, text or object from which we gather information about a past event or period.

Students study the taxonomy diagram in the textbook. The teacher walks through each branch: Archaeological Sources (monuments, mounds, excavated tools, weapons, figurines, pottery, burials); Inscriptions (manuscripts, copper plates, coins); Oral Sources (genealogies, folklore); Indian Literature (Vedas, Itihasas, poems, scientific texts); Foreign Accounts (travelogues, chronicles); Artistic Sources (paintings, sculptures, panels). For each branch, students write one concrete example in their own words.

Groups of three are each given one of the six source categories. Each group produces a quick-reference card — on one half of their notebook page — listing the sub-types, one real-world example, and one type of historical question their category can answer (e.g., Artistic Sources can answer: what clothing did people wear?). Groups have a fixed working period, then one member reads the card aloud.

The teacher poses: 'If an archaeologist finds pottery at a site but foreign accounts say that region had no settlements at that time, what do historians do?' Students discuss the principle of cross-checking and the need to judge which source is more reliable. The teacher notes that scientific methods — climate studies, chemical analysis, genetic studies — are increasingly used alongside these conventional categories.

periods.section_context: Six-category taxonomy: archaeological, inscriptions, oral, Indian literature, foreign accounts, artistic sources
periods.teacher_notes: The section introduces the full taxonomy of sources as the conceptual core of the chapter's second major question. Students commonly conflate inscriptions with manuscripts — clarify that copper plates and coins are inscriptional sources because they carry written records, distinct from the broader manuscript tradition.

competency_edges.competency_text: Collecting and interpreting multiple sources of information to understand historical aspects of human life
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can classify historical evidence into the six-category taxonomy and explain what type of historical question each source category can and cannot answer.

periods.section_anchor: What Are the Sources of History?
materials: Textbook images of artefacts: coin, carved panel, Ashoka lion capital
Notebook or worksheet for written responses
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images: a coin, a carved panel, and the Ashoka lion capital

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly names the three artefacts visible in the textbook — the coin, the carved panel and the Ashoka lion capital — and asks students to identify which source category from the taxonomy each belongs to before examining them closely. This activates the classification work from the prior unit on the taxonomy.

Working individually, students write a response to each artefact using a three-prompt scaffold: (1) What can you directly observe on this object? (2) What does that observation tell you about the people who made or used it — their technology, beliefs, political authority or trade? (3) What question about this object can you not answer from the object alone, and what other source type might help? Students complete all three prompts for all three artefacts.

Pairs share their responses to the Ashoka lion capital specifically. The teacher draws out that a single artefact can carry evidence about political authority (a state symbol), artistic tradition (sculptural style), religious affiliation (Buddhist context) and language (inscriptions on the pillar elsewhere). This illustrates how one object speaks to multiple historical questions.

The teacher asks: 'When a coin and a travelogue give conflicting information about a ruler, how do historians decide which to trust?' Students name factors — which source is closer in time to the event, who produced it and why, whether other sources corroborate it. The teacher frames this as the historian's judgement problem, not a simple rule.

periods.section_context: Coin, carved panel, Ashoka lion capital; cross-checking and reliability of sources
periods.teacher_notes: This unit applies the taxonomy from the sources section to real artefacts, asking students to move from identification to interpretation and then to recognise the limits of a single source. A common error is treating the artefact as self-explanatory — the third scaffold prompt (what question can you not answer?) is designed to break that habit. The Ashoka lion capital is rich enough to carry all three prompt levels and is worth dwelling on.

competency_edges.competency_text: Collecting and interpreting multiple sources of information to understand historical aspects of human life
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can extract historical information from a physical artefact, identify the limits of that source, and propose a complementary source type to fill the gap.

periods.activity_title: Hunter-Gatherers: Evidence of Early Human Life
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of a rock shelter with rock paintings

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: 'Modern humans — Homo sapiens — appeared about 300,000 years ago. Using the timeline skills from the work on CE/BCE and centuries, how many centuries is that? How many millennia?' Students calculate. The teacher then asks what kind of evidence we could possibly have about people who left no written records, prompting students to name relevant source categories from the taxonomy.

Students read the section on early human life and complete a four-column evidence table: Evidence type | What it is (specific example from the text) | What it tells us about early human life | Which scholar studies it. Examples include stone axes and arrowheads (tools studied by archaeologists), shell bead ornaments (trade and social networks), rock paintings depicting animals and humans (communication and art), and fire (technology and shelter). Students work individually, then compare with a partner.

The teacher displays the rock shelter illustration from the textbook. Students examine it and answer: (1) What activities can you see or infer are happening? (2) What materials and technologies are present? (3) What does this shelter tell you about how these people organised their daily lives — food, safety, social grouping? Students write responses and share two observations with the class.

The teacher poses the Think About It question: 'The illustration shows certain people doing certain tasks — do you think those role assignments were fixed, or might men and women have shared different tasks in different groups?' Students offer brief responses, noting that rock paintings worldwide show varied roles. This sets up the gender-reflection thread that the chapter carries forward.

periods.section_context: Homo sapiens 300,000 years ago, hunter-gatherer bands, stone tools, rock paintings, ornament exchange
periods.teacher_notes: Having traced the deep timeline and source taxonomy in earlier units, this unit applies both to the concrete evidence of early human life. Students often assume rock paintings are purely decorative — push them to see that paintings depicting hunting scenes, animal movements or group gatherings are a form of communication and possibly record-keeping. The calculation of how many centuries ago Homo sapiens appeared links back to the CE/BCE and millennium skills and keeps those tools active.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing the causal arc from early Homo sapiens hunter-gatherer life through the post-Ice Age transition to settled communities
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify and categorise multiple forms of evidence for early hunter-gatherer life and explain what each reveals about nomadic social organisation.

periods.activity_title: From Ice Age to the First Settlements
materials: Textbook illustration of an agricultural community
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of an early agricultural community several millennia ago

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students to visualise the Ice Age: most of the Earth is covered in ice; rivers are frozen. Then the climate warms — what changes? Students predict: ice melts, rivers swell, land becomes habitable, plants grow. The teacher adds the textbook's framing: the last Ice Age lasted from over 100,000 years ago to around 12,000 years ago. Students mark both dates on the BCE side of the number line they built in earlier timeline work.

Students read the section on the first crops and construct a cause-effect chain with at least five links: climate warms → ice melts, rivers swell → fertile land near rivers becomes available → humans cultivate cereals and domesticate cattle and goats → food supply grows and communities expand → settlements form near rivers. For each link, students write one piece of evidence or reasoning from the text that supports it.

The teacher displays the illustration of the agricultural community. Students examine it and answer: (1) What crops or animals can you identify? (2) What technologies are present — do you see pottery or metal tools? (3) How is this community's daily life different from the hunter-gatherer rock shelter? Students write a comparison of at least three differences.

The class discusses: 'Why did communities settle near rivers rather than inland?' Students name water for crops, fertile soil from river deposits and ease of communication. The teacher then asks: 'As villages grew into towns, what new social and organisational challenges would arise?' Students suggest the emergence of leaders, division of labour and trade — setting up the social complexity thread.

periods.section_context: Last Ice Age to 12,000 years ago, cereal cultivation, river settlements, cause-effect chain of transition
periods.teacher_notes: The transition from nomadic hunter-gatherer life to settled agriculture is the key causal arc this section tracks; the cause-effect chain task makes that arc explicit rather than leaving it as background narrative. Students often treat the warming of the climate as a simple coincidence — emphasise that it is the trigger that made settled life possible in many parts of the world simultaneously.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing the causal arc from early Homo sapiens hunter-gatherer life through the post-Ice Age transition to settled communities
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct a cause-effect chain linking post-Ice Age climate change to the emergence of settled agricultural communities near rivers.

time_bands.activity: The teacher recalls the cause-effect chain of the previous unit — climate warms, settlements form near rivers — and asks: 'Once a hamlet of twenty families grows into a village of two hundred, what new problems appear?' Students suggest food storage, dispute resolution, distributing tools and coordinating planting. This surfaces the social complexity thread organically.

Students read the section's account of social development and complete a growth-sequence diagram with three columns — Hamlet, Village, Town — listing for each: approximate size, how food is obtained and shared, what technology is available, and what social role or institution has emerged (collective cultivation without individual ownership → chieftains overseeing welfare → networks of trade and communication). Students fill the diagram from the text.

The teacher introduces pottery and metallurgy: pottery enabled storage and cooking of surplus grain; copper metallurgy (and later iron) produced durable tools, everyday objects and ornaments. Students write two explanations: (1) How did pottery change the way communities handled surplus food? (2) How did copper tools change what kinds of work communities could do? These must use the vocabulary of the section — surplus, durability, trade, ornament.

The Think About It activity: the teacher asks students to look at both the rock shelter and agricultural illustrations and reflect — 'Who is shown doing which tasks? Could those roles have been different? What evidence from rock paintings or elsewhere suggests women also painted or men also cooked?' Students write two sentences of critical reflection. The unit closes by noting that the chapter describes this early progress as preparing the ground for the emergence of civilisation.

periods.section_context: Hamlet-to-village-to-town growth, collective cultivation, chieftains, pottery, copper metallurgy, gender roles
periods.teacher_notes: Building on the transition from nomadic life and the emergence of river settlements, this unit examines the social and technological elaboration that followed. A common confusion is that metallurgy began with iron — the text is explicit that copper came first and iron came later, which is worth emphasising. The gender-role reflection at the close is an issues-based prompt the chapter explicitly raises; handle it as a genuine open question rather than leading students to a predetermined answer.

competency_edges.competency_text: Tracing the causal arc from early Homo sapiens hunter-gatherer life through the post-Ice Age transition to settled communities
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace the sequence from hamlet to village to town, linking each stage to specific social structures and technological innovations.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identifying and critically questioning gender-based assumptions in historical depictions
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can identify assumed gender roles in historical scenes and generate counter-examples that question whether those roles were universal or fixed.

periods.activity_title: Sources, Scholars and the Story of Early Humanity
periods.section_anchor: How Do We Learn About the Past? / What Are the Sources of History? / The Beginnings of Human History / The First Crops

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses four rapid-fire questions — one for each major section — to gauge recall: (1) Name one scholar who studies fossils and one who excavates tools. (2) If an event happened in 200 BCE and another in 300 CE, how many years separate them? (3) Name two types of archaeological sources. (4) What change in climate triggered the shift from nomadic to settled life? Students answer on their mini-boards or in their notebooks; the teacher corrects errors immediately.

Students choose one of three extended-response tasks: (A) Explain how a historian would use three different source types — one archaeological, one literary, one artistic — to reconstruct daily life in an early settlement near a river. What would each source reveal, and what would it leave unanswered? (B) Construct an annotated timeline from 300,000 BCE to 2025 CE that marks at least six events from the chapter, correctly labelled with CE or BCE and their correct century. For each event, name the source type that provides evidence. (C) A chieftain in an early village wants to expand agriculture. Identify two social challenges the community would face and explain, using the chapter's evidence, how early technologies (pottery, copper tools) might address them.

Students write their chosen response individually. The teacher circulates, prompting with: 'What specific source from the taxonomy supports that claim?' or 'Which direction does BCE count — does a larger BCE number mean more recent or older?' Responses must name specific content from the chapter, not general statements.

Two or three students read one key sentence from their response. The teacher draws the chapter to a close by naming the thread that connects all four sections: the tools historians use to know the past, the systems they use to date it, the evidence that survives from the very earliest humans, and the long slow transition that produced the first civilisations — a story told from evidence, always incomplete, always open to new sources.

periods.section_context: Cross-chapter consolidation: scholars, CE/BCE calculation, source taxonomy, hunter-gatherers, agricultural transition
periods.teacher_notes: This unit consolidates the full arc of the chapter — the scholars and deep timeline, the CE/BCE and century system, the six-category source taxonomy, the hunter-gatherer evidence base and the agricultural transition — through differentiated extended response tasks rather than a summary lecture. A common gap at this stage is students who can name source categories but cannot apply them to a specific historical situation; the task options are designed to force that application. All three task options are equivalent in demand and students should be encouraged to choose the one that plays to their strengths.

competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can select and apply multiple source types from the taxonomy to reconstruct a historical situation, naming what each source reveals and what it leaves unresolved.

competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct an annotated multi-event timeline spanning BCE and CE, correctly applying century labels and linking each event to its evidential source.

assessment_items.chapter_section: What Are the Sources of History?
assessment_items.question_text: A historian finds a copper plate with writing engraved on it, describing a king's land grant. Into which category of historical sources does this object fall?

options.label: A
options.text: Archaeological Sources

options.label: B
options.text: Foreign Accounts

options.label: C
options.text: Inscriptions

options.label: D
options.text: Oral Sources

assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may point to the object rather than write the category label if motor difficulties are present.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses any excavated or physical object with the archaeological sub-category, not recognising that written records on objects form their own inscriptional category.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses written records with oral transmission, possibly because both involve language.
what_each_option_reveals.B: May associate written sources broadly with foreign accounts, not distinguishing source type by origin and medium.

competency.competency_text: Collecting and interpreting multiple sources of information to understand historical aspects of human life

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can extract historical information from a physical artefact, identify the limits of that source, and propose a complementary source type to fill the gap.
assessment_items.chapter_section: What Are the Sources of History?
assessment_items.question_text: An archaeologist excavates a coin bearing a ruler's portrait and a symbol. She can use this coin to identify the ruler's likely identity and the period of the coin's minting. Which question about this ruler CANNOT be answered from the coin alone?

options.label: A
options.text: Approximately when did the ruler govern?

options.label: B
options.text: What did the ruler look like?

options.label: C
options.text: What laws did the ruler issue during their reign?

options.label: D
options.text: What symbol was associated with the ruler's authority?

what_each_option_reveals.B: Fails to recognise that a portrait on a coin directly conveys appearance; does not distinguish between answerable and unanswerable questions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Fails to recognise that symbols on a coin are direct evidence of authority iconography; confuses the question of limits with questions of iconographic interpretation.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Does not recognise that coin style and metal composition can be used to date a reign approximately; conflates 'difficult' with 'impossible'.

assessment_items.chapter_section: What Are the Sources of History?
assessment_items.question_text: A historian is trying to understand the religious beliefs of people who lived in an ancient Indian city. She has two sources: (i) a sculpture showing a deity found at the site, and (ii) a chapter from an ancient Sanskrit text describing rituals. Name the source category each belongs to. Then explain one historical question each source can answer that the other cannot.
expected_elements: Correctly names the sculpture as an Artistic Source (or Archaeological Source — sculptures can appear under either; accept either with justification).
Correctly names the Sanskrit text as Indian Literature.
States at least one question the sculpture can answer that the text cannot — for example, questions about the physical form in which the deity was depicted, or the artistic style of the period.
States at least one question the text can answer that the sculpture cannot — for example, the sequence or language of rituals, or the names and roles of deities.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may draw a simple two-column table rather than write in prose if that supports their expression.

assessment_items.chapter_section: What Are the Sources of History?
assessment_items.question_text: A historian wants to understand daily life in an early settlement near a river in ancient India — what people ate, what tools they used, what they believed, and how they were governed. Explain how three different source types from the taxonomy (choose three from: archaeological, inscriptional, oral, Indian literature, foreign accounts, artistic) would each contribute to this reconstruction. For each source type, state what it reveals AND what gap it leaves that another type must fill.
look_for: Names three distinct source categories from the taxonomy correctly.

competency.competency_text: Collecting and interpreting multiple sources of information to understand historical aspects of human life

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can select and apply multiple source types from the taxonomy to reconstruct a historical situation, naming what each source reveals and what it leaves unresolved.
assessment_items.chapter_section: What Are the Sources of History?
assessment_items.task: You are a historian investigating life in an early river-bank settlement. Three items have been found at the site: a clay pot with charred grain inside, a carved stone panel showing people working in a field, and a fragment of copper. Create a source analysis task: for each item, write two structured questions — one asking what historical information the item directly provides, and one asking what further source would be needed to answer a question the item leaves open. Then write a short paragraph explaining why no single source is enough to reconstruct the full picture of life in this settlement.
assessment_items.scaffold: For each item, answer: (1) What does this object directly tell us about life in the settlement? Name the specific source category it belongs to. (2) What is one important question about the settlement that this object cannot answer? Which other source type from the taxonomy would help answer it? After completing all three items, write 3–4 sentences: Why do historians need to use several different types of sources together? Use at least two examples from your analysis above.
format_of_output: Three pairs of structured questions (one pair per item), each clearly labelled with the item name and source category
A concluding paragraph of 3–4 sentences explaining the need for multiple sources, using specific examples from the student's own analysis
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who find extended writing difficult may use a table for the three-item analysis and write only the concluding paragraph in prose.

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Students demonstrate the ability to read physical objects as historical evidence, classify them within the source taxonomy, identify the limits of each source, and articulate why historians triangulate across multiple source types.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The two-question structure for each item ensures students engage with both what a source reveals (classification and interpretation) and what it cannot reveal (gap identification). The concluding paragraph requires generalisation — the transfer move that distinguishes evaluation from mere application.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses name specific information each object provides (e.g., charred grain in the pot → evidence of grain storage or cooking), correctly assign source categories, and identify a genuine gap with a plausible complementary source. The concluding paragraph makes a principled argument about source limitation, not just a list. Weak responses treat the objects as interchangeable, fail to identify real gaps, or write a concluding paragraph that merely repeats the three descriptions without generalising.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Source analysis task (2–3 structured questions on a provided short source)
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The source analysis format is the most natural demonstration vehicle for this LO because the competency requires students to apply the interpretive and gap-identification skills that the taxonomy unit and artefact analysis unit built — exactly the operation a structured source analysis task elicits. The teacher may substitute any other format from the Open Task menu.

competency.competency_text: Representing and analysing historical data in timeline form, including CE/BCE date calculation

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct a number-line timeline, position dated events correctly in CE and BCE, and calculate elapsed time across the CE/BCE boundary.
assessment_items.chapter_section: How Is Time Measured in History?
assessment_items.question_text: Gautama Buddha was born approximately in 560 BCE. India gained independence in 1947 CE. Applying the rule that there is no year zero in the Gregorian calendar, how many years separate these two events?

options.label: A
options.text: 1387 years

options.label: B
options.text: 2505 years

options.label: C
options.text: 2506 years

options.label: D
options.text: 2507 years

what_each_option_reveals.A: Subtracts the smaller from the larger without crossing the BCE/CE boundary — treats both dates as if they were on the same side of the number line.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Adds 560 and 1947 without subtracting 1 for the missing year zero — applies the cross-boundary rule partially.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Subtracts 2 rather than 1 for the year-zero correction — misremembers the formula as subtract 2.

competency.competency_text: Representing and analysing historical data in timeline form, including CE/BCE date calculation

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can place events on a scaled timeline, assign century labels, and assess the reliability of the source behind each placement.
assessment_items.chapter_section: How Is Time Measured in History?
assessment_items.question_text: A student building a family timeline finds that her great-grandmother was born 'sometime in the early 1920s', based on a relative's memory. She places the birth at exactly 1921 CE and labels it as being in the 20th century. Which of the following best describes the reliability problem with this timeline entry?

options.label: A
options.text: Oral memories cannot be used as sources at all in timeline construction.

options.label: B
options.text: The century label is wrong — 1921 CE falls in the 19th century.

options.label: C
options.text: The entry is fully reliable because the student used a primary source.

options.label: D
options.text: The exact year is uncertain because the source is an oral memory, not a document; the century label is correct.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses century-counting — does not know that the 20th century runs from 1901 to 2000 CE.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Over-generalises from the reliability limitation of oral sources to a blanket exclusion — does not recognise oral sources as a valid category in the taxonomy.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Conflates 'family member as source' with 'primary source' and does not question the precision of the date derived from an imprecise memory.

competency.competency_text: Tracing the causal arc from early Homo sapiens hunter-gatherer life through the post-Ice Age transition to settled communities

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and categorise multiple forms of evidence for early hunter-gatherer life and explain what each reveals about nomadic social organisation.
assessment_items.question_text: Archaeologists have found shell bead ornaments at sites hundreds of kilometres apart, dating to the same period of early human prehistory. What does this evidence most directly reveal about early hunter-gatherer groups?

options.label: A
options.text: Early humans had contact and exchange networks across distances.

options.label: B
options.text: Early humans had developed metallurgy by this period.

options.label: C
options.text: Early humans lived permanently near the sea.

options.label: D
options.text: Early humans used shells only for decoration, not for tools.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses the material (shells from the sea) with the location of habitation — does not reason that shells can be carried far from where they were collected.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Draws an unfounded negative inference from the material type, ignoring the text's explicit statement that stone tools were also made.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses the technological period — metallurgy began much later, with copper, and is associated with settled communities rather than hunter-gatherers.

competency.competency_text: Tracing the causal arc from early Homo sapiens hunter-gatherer life through the post-Ice Age transition to settled communities

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct a cause-effect chain linking post-Ice Age climate change to the emergence of settled agricultural communities near rivers.
assessment_items.question_text: After the last Ice Age ended around 12,000 years ago, early humans in many parts of the world began settling near rivers. Which sequence of causes and effects best explains this shift?

options.label: A
options.text: Climate warmed → ice melted → rivers swelled and deposited fertile soil → humans settled near rivers to cultivate cereals.

options.label: B
options.text: Humans first built towns → towns needed water → they moved to rivers → agriculture developed as a result.

options.label: C
options.text: Pottery was invented → pottery needed clay from riverbeds → humans settled near rivers → farming followed.

options.label: D
options.text: Rivers froze → humans moved to higher ground → they discovered agriculture on plateaus → they returned to rivers later.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Reverses the cause — describes the Ice Age condition rather than the post-Ice Age warming; misunderstands the direction of the climatic trigger.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Inverts the causal sequence — treats towns as pre-existing agriculture rather than as a later development arising from it.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Assigns pottery as the primary cause of river settlement, confusing a technology that emerged alongside settled life with the climate trigger that made settlement possible.

competency.competency_text: Tracing the causal arc from early Homo sapiens hunter-gatherer life through the post-Ice Age transition to settled communities

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace the sequence from hamlet to village to town, linking each stage to specific social structures and technological innovations.
assessment_items.question_text: Early agricultural communities grew from small hamlets into villages and eventually into small towns. Describe two changes — one social and one technological — that accompanied this growth. For each change, explain why it was needed at that stage of community development.
expected_elements: Names a specific social change — for example, the emergence of chieftains or leaders to oversee community welfare; or the shift from collective land cultivation without individual ownership to coordinated land management.
Explains why that social change was needed — for example, as community size grew, someone was needed to coordinate distribution of food or resolve disputes.
Names a specific technological change — for example, pottery enabling storage of surplus grain; or copper metallurgy enabling production of durable tools and ornaments.
Explains why that technological change was needed — for example, surplus food required storage vessels; harder metal tools made agricultural work and craft production more efficient.
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may use bullet points rather than full paragraphs; the quality of the causal explanation matters more than prose form.

competency.competency_text: Identifying and critically questioning gender-based assumptions in historical depictions

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify assumed gender roles in historical scenes and generate counter-examples that question whether those roles were universal or fixed.
assessment_items.question_text: An illustration of an early agricultural community shows men ploughing fields while women cook near a dwelling. A student says: 'This proves that in early human societies, farming was always done by men.' Which response best challenges this claim?

options.label: A
options.text: An illustration reflects the choices of the person who drew it and may not represent all situations; rock paintings and other evidence suggest both men and women performed a range of tasks.

options.label: B
options.text: Farming roles are determined by physical strength, so the illustration is accurate.

options.label: C
options.text: The claim would be correct if confirmed by a single travelogue from the same period.

options.label: D
options.text: The student is correct because all early agricultural illustrations show the same pattern.

assessment_items.inclusivity: Read the stem aloud for students who benefit from auditory support.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Accepts the generalisation uncritically and adds a false claim about all illustrations — does not apply any critical questioning.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Treats a single travelogue as definitive confirmation — does not apply the principle of cross-checking multiple sources or questioning the bias of any single source.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Rationalises the gender assignment with a physical determinism argument — substitutes a biological claim for historical evidence, exactly the kind of naturalisation the Think About It box critiques.

competency.competency_text: Identifying and critically questioning gender-based assumptions in historical depictions

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify assumed gender roles in historical scenes and generate counter-examples that question whether those roles were universal or fixed.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter's Think About It activity points out that images of early human life often show women doing particular tasks and men doing others, but notes these depictions 'are not necessarily accurate and do not cover all situations'. Which of the following is the best example of the kind of counter-evidence the chapter offers?

options.label: A
options.text: Modern societies divide tasks the same way, confirming the historical pattern.

options.label: B
options.text: No counter-evidence exists because archaeology cannot record gender.

options.label: C
options.text: Rock paintings from some sites show women painting or men performing domestic tasks.

options.label: D
options.text: Written records from the same period confirm the roles shown.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Invokes written records as confirmation rather than questioning the depiction — does not engage with the chapter's critical stance on assumed roles.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Uses a presentism argument — projects current patterns back onto early human societies — rather than engaging with actual prehistoric evidence.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Overstates the limits of archaeology — the chapter itself offers rock painting evidence as a counter-example, so this claim is factually wrong.
